Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

1. Background and purpose

Harbor Street Neighbors began discussing a coat swap in early October after several residents asked where they could donate children’s winter clothing in usable condition. The group’s notes describe the event as a way to help local households find warm coats without requiring a purchase, while also keeping wearable items in use. It was not planned as a general clothing drive. The organizers chose to focus on coats, snow pants, hats, mittens, and scarves because those were the items residents had specifically asked about. The notes do not say that every visitor would receive an item, or that the group had enough clothing for all expected demand.

2. Date, place, and access

The swap was scheduled for Saturday, November 16, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. in the downstairs meeting room at Harbor Street Library. The room entrance is on the east side of the building, beside the public garden. The library’s main entrance has steps, while the east entrance has a ramp. Organizers planned to put up temporary signs outside and in the lobby, subject to the library’s approval. The meeting room is normally used for community programs, and the library requested that tables be moved back into their usual positions before closing. The notes identify the event as free and open to anyone, not just library members or Harbor Street residents.

3. Collection and item condition

Residents were invited to bring clean, wearable winter items to the library on Friday, November 15, between 4 and 7 p.m., or to arrange an earlier drop-off with volunteer coordinator Mina Patel. The collection note asks people to check pockets and label items that need a minor repair. Coats with broken zippers were not automatically excluded, but the organizers said they could not promise to repair them. Items that were wet, heavily stained, or missing essential fasteners were not to be put out for visitors. A note from volunteer Luis Romero says, “If you would not hand it to a friend to wear, please leave it at home.” The group had not decided where unusable donations would go.

4. Sorting and selection

Volunteers planned to sort items by approximate size and type, with separate areas for adult coats, children’s coats, snow pants, and accessories. The notes say that size labels on clothing are inconsistent, so volunteers would also use a tape measure for a few garments when practical. Visitors could browse and try on coats in the library’s washroom, but there was no planned fitting-room area. Organizers expected to have a few mirrors and a folding screen, although the source notes do not confirm whether the library had approved those items. Visitors were asked to take only what they or someone in their household could use that winter; there was no stated numerical limit per person.

5. Volunteer roles and supplies

Mina Patel was coordinating drop-offs and the volunteer schedule. Luis Romero was preparing signs and checking the tables, while library staff member Dana Brooks was the point of contact for access to the room. The draft schedule listed two volunteers for setup at 8:45 a.m., three people to greet visitors, and at least two people to keep the size areas tidy. The notes do not provide a complete shift roster. Requested supplies included clothing racks, hangers, paper size markers, painter’s tape, a small repair kit, and bags for visitors who needed them. One resident offered two portable racks, but the notes do not confirm that either rack had been delivered.

6. Communication and attendance

A neighborhood email dated November 4 announced the event and invited both donations and visitors. The organizers planned to post the same information on the library bulletin board and the Harbor Street Neighbors page. They estimated that 30 to 50 people might attend, based on turnout at earlier neighborhood events, but the estimate was not a registration count. The email included the library address and event hours but did not mention whether visitors needed to bring identification. In a reply, resident Omar Greene asked, “Can I bring a coat for my teenager and still look for one for my younger child?” Mina answered that households could bring items and browse for what they needed, while noting that availability would depend on donations.

7. Weather and changes

The planning notes say the event would remain indoors. If heavy snow made the library close, the swap would be postponed, but the notes do not name a backup date. Dana Brooks said that the library would post a closure notice through its usual channels. A separate message suggested moving the event to the following Saturday if the room became unavailable for another reason; this was raised as an option, not recorded as an agreed plan. The organizers also had not decided whether any leftover usable coats would be stored for a later event, offered to another local group, or returned to donors. The notes indicate that Mina intended to ask volunteers about storage space after the swap.

8. Follow-up

The draft plan included counting the remaining coats and accessories at the end of the event, then recording general totals rather than names of visitors. No sign-in sheet was planned. The group wanted to thank the library and volunteers in a neighborhood message the following week. The notes do not report how many items were collected, how many visitors attended, whether the event took place as scheduled, or what happened to leftover items.
